certification.name: PyTorch Core: Practical ML & Neural Networks

concepts.name: Selecting an accelerator
concepts.description: Current PyTorch provides `torch.accelerator` APIs to query an available accelerator such as CUDA, MPS, XPU, or other supported backends.

concepts.name: Move model and data together
concepts.description: `model.to(device)` moves registered model parameters and buffers, while input tensors usually need their own `.to(device)` call.

concepts.name: Saving model weights
concepts.description: A recommended PyTorch pattern saves `model.state_dict()` rather than serializing the entire Python model object.

concepts.name: Loading model weights
concepts.description: To restore a state dict, recreate the model architecture and call `model.load_state_dict(...)` with the loaded mapping.

concepts.name: Training checkpoints
concepts.description: A resumable training checkpoint commonly stores the model state dict, optimizer state dict, current epoch or step, and other training state you need to continue.

concepts.name: Automatic mixed precision autocast
concepts.description: `torch.autocast` runs eligible operations in selected lower precision while keeping other operations in higher precision as appropriate.

concepts.name: Gradient scaling for float16 AMP
concepts.description: `torch.amp.GradScaler` scales the loss and gradients to reduce float16 gradient underflow during mixed-precision training.

concepts.name: `torch.compile`
concepts.description: `torch.compile` returns an optimized callable around a model or Python function using PyTorch compilation infrastructure.

concepts.name: Reproducibility and determinism
concepts.description: Reproducible PyTorch experiments often begin by seeding random generators, while stricter determinism may require additional backend or algorithm settings.

questions.explanation: Current PyTorch provides torch.accelerator APIs to query an available accelerator such as CUDA, MPS, XPU, or other supported backends. A current quickstart pattern uses the available accelerator when present and otherwise falls back to CPU. Selecting a device is only part of the job; model parameters and input tensors must also be moved to that device.

content.template:
model = model.{{model_method}}(device)

for X, y in train_loader:
    X = X.{{tensor_method}}(device)
    y = y.to(device)
    logits = model(X)

questions.explanation: model.to(device) moves registered model parameters and buffers, while input tensors usually need their own .to(device) call. Move both model and batch tensors to compatible devices before running operations between them. Moving only the model or only the data commonly causes device-mismatch errors.
hints: Move both model and batch tensors to compatible devices before running operations between them.

questions.explanation: A resumable training checkpoint commonly stores the model state dict, optimizer state dict, current epoch or step, and other training state you need to continue. Optimizer state matters because adaptive optimizers and momentum methods keep internal state beyond model weights. Saving only model weights is enough for inference but may not reproduce a seamless training resume.

questions.explanation: torch.autocast runs eligible operations in selected lower precision while keeping other operations in higher precision as appropriate. Wrap the forward pass and loss computation in an autocast context when using automatic mixed precision. Do not place backward itself inside autocast; backward uses the dtypes chosen for the corresponding forward operations.
hints: Wrap the forward pass and loss computation in an autocast context when using automatic mixed precision.

questions.explanation: torch.amp.GradScaler scales the loss and gradients to reduce float16 gradient underflow during mixed-precision training. A common CUDA sequence is scaler.scale(loss).backward(), scaler.step(optimizer), then scaler.update(). GradScaler is not required for ordinary full-precision training and is not needed for inference-only autocast.

questions.explanation: torch.compile returns an optimized callable around a model or Python function using PyTorch compilation infrastructure. A simple entry point is compiled_model = torch.compile(model) and then calling the compiled model normally. Compilation can add startup overhead and graph breaks, so measure end-to-end performance instead of assuming every workload becomes faster.
hints: A simple entry point is compiled_model = torch.compile(model) and then calling the compiled model normally.
